items.prose: `wc -l` does not really count lines. It counts newline characters, the invisible end-of-line marks, written `"\n"` in Python. A last line with no newline after it is not counted. Finish the function so it gives the same number as `wc -l`.
items.question: Complete `wc_l(text)`.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests, including an empty file and a last line with no newline. Each result must equal the expected whole number.

feedback.correct: Your function counts newlines, exactly as wc -l does.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count only the newline characters.

explain.text: Inside the loop, `if ch == "\n": count += 1` adds one per newline. A file whose last line lacks a newline gets one fewer than you might expect. `text.count("\n")` does the same in one step.

The manual for wc includes these lines:

```sh
-l    count lines
-w    count words: runs of characters
      between spaces, tabs or newlines
-c    count bytes
```

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The manual says what separates words.

byKey.commas: You split on commas. wc only splits on spaces, tabs and newlines, so each CSV line is one word.

items.title: Set up a dataset, safely
items.prompt:
Your terminal has just opened, and you do not know which folder it is in. ~/Downloads holds spx.csv: daily S&P 500 closes, one header line, then one line per day. Dates look like 2023-01-03. Write the commands, one per line, each with a short reason, to do the following.
1. Make a folder ~/projects/spx.
2. Copy spx.csv into it, keeping the original.
3. Find how many trading days the file holds.
4. Save the header and the 2023 rows into spx_2023.csv inside the project.
5. Check how many 2023 days you have.
6. Name one mistake with `>` and one with `rm -r` that would lose data here, and how you would avoid each.
items.model:
**Commands.**

```sh
$ mkdir ~/projects/spx
$ cd ~/projects/spx
$ cp ~/Downloads/spx.csv .
$ wc -l spx.csv
$ head -n 1 spx.csv > spx_2023.csv
$ grep 2023- spx.csv >> spx_2023.csv
$ wc -l spx_2023.csv
```

**Reasons.** `mkdir` with a `~` path works from any starting folder, so I do not need to know where the terminal opened. `cd` puts me in the project, so later names are short and point where I mean. `cp`, not `mv`, keeps the download; the dot means this folder. `wc -l` counts lines, so the number of trading days is that count minus 1 for the header. `head -n 1 ... >` starts the new file with the header, because grep alone would drop it. `grep 2023-` keeps lines containing 2023-, which only the 2023 dates do. `>>` adds them below the header rather than wiping it. The final `wc -l`, minus 1, is the number of 2023 trading days, about 250.

**Mistake with >.** Writing `grep 2023- spx.csv > spx.csv` empties spx.csv before grep reads it, so the data is gone. Using `>` on the grep line, instead of `>>`, wipes the header I just wrote. I avoid both by writing to a new file name and using `>>` to add.

**Mistake with rm -r.** Tidying up with `rm -r spx` from the wrong folder deletes the wrong thing. There is no Bin and no undo. Before any `rm -r` I run `pwd` and `ls` on the exact name I am about to delete.

rubric.text: Makes the folder with a path that works from any starting folder, such as `~/projects/spx`
Copies with `cp`, not `mv`, so the original download stays
Uses `wc -l` and subtracts 1 for the header to get the number of trading days
Writes the header with `>` first, then adds the 2023 rows with `>>`, in that order
Chooses search text, such as `2023-`, that matches only 2023 dates
Checks the result with `wc -l` and subtracts the header
Names a real `>` mistake (redirecting onto the input file, or `>` instead of `>>`) and a fix
Names the `rm -r` wrong-folder risk and checks `pwd` and `ls` first
